# Two Years On: Follow-up of the Varden County Trial and a Subset of Halden Pilot Organisations

*Field report. A. Lindqvist, P. Mahony, D. Rao (Varden County Evaluation Unit / Easterly University) and R. Okafor (Halden Institute for Work Studies). Registered follow-up protocol VC-2023-04-F, filed at month 11.*

## Summary

We report 24-month outcomes from two sources: the Varden County cluster-randomised trial, whose case-processing offices remained on their assigned schedules for two years, and 14 organisations from the Halden pilot that hold record-based output data. In Varden case-processing offices, the gain in output per actual hour relative to control fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months, measured with system log data, and output per employee stood at −3.4% (95% CI −8.0 to +1.2). The gain has therefore declined but not disappeared. A registered mediation test confirms that the reduction in recurring meetings accounts for 47% (95% CI 28 to 66%) of the per-hour gain; improved fatigue accounts for 18% (2 to 34%). The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12 because of waiting times. Three of the 14 Halden organisations have reverted, all with client-facing or coverage obligations.

## 1. Background

The nine-month report of the Varden trial left three questions to be settled at follow-up: whether the per-hour gain in case-processing would persist; whether the meetings association, found in an unregistered analysis, would survive a registered test; and whether timesheets understated the work actually done. Two subsequent publications bear on the first two. A re-analysis of the Halden pilot argued that per-hour gains in reduced-hours schemes are entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the meetings hypothesis was a post hoc story. A meta-analysis of 23 studies concluded that effects show no sign of decay, on the basis of four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months. We address each directly.

## 2. Varden County: design at 24 months

The seven treated and seven control case-processing offices kept their assigned schedules for 24 months. To address concern about unrecorded work, we added a second hours measure: active log-in time on the county's case-management system, which records time staff are working on cases whether or not they claim it on a timesheet. The mediation analysis was registered at month 11, before 24-month outcomes were available. It specified two mediators, weekly hours in recurring meetings (from calendar data) and a validated fatigue scale, and a single outcome, output per log-measured hour.

The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12. In months 10 to 12, average waiting time in treated counter offices was 7.3 minutes against 4.0 in control offices, and the county judged that restoring service would require 12% more staff, raising the cost per contact handled by an estimated 9%. Those offices returned to 37.5 hours.

## 3. Varden County: results

**Table 1. Case-processing offices, treated relative to control (difference-in-differences)**

| Outcome | 9 months | 24 months |
|---|---|---|
| Output per FTE | −2.1% (−6.8 to +2.6) | −3.4% (−8.0 to +1.2) |
| Actual hours, timesheets | −13% | −12% |
| Actual hours, system logs | — | −11% |
| Output per hour, timesheets | +12.5% (+6.9 to +18.4) | +9.8% (+4.6 to +15.2) |
| Output per hour, system logs | — | +8.5% (+3.4 to +13.8) |
| Appeal overturn rate (treated v control) | 3.1% v 3.0% | 3.2% v 3.0% |
| Sick days per FTE | −29% | −27% |
| Annual resignations (treated v control) | 3.9% v 7.4% | 4.1% v 7.9% |

Log data show slightly more work than timesheets: actual hours fell by 11% on logs and 12% on timesheets, so the per-hour gain on the stricter measure is 8.5%. That gain is smaller than at nine months but its confidence interval excludes zero by a clear margin. Output per employee remains slightly below control; the hours reduction is mostly, not fully, offset.

The decline from 12.5% to 9.8% on the like-for-like timesheet measure is consistent with some fading of an initial effect. It is not consistent with the gain falling to zero by month ten, as an extrapolation of self-reported energy in the Halden data had suggested.

### Mediation

Recurring meeting time in treated case-processing offices fell from 7.4 to 3.9 hours per week per person between baseline and month 24; in control offices it moved from 7.2 to 7.0. Fatigue scores improved by 0.34 standard deviations in treated offices relative to control.

**Table 2. Registered mediation analysis, output per log-measured hour, 24 months**

| Pathway | Share of per-hour gain explained (95% CI) |
|---|---|
| Reduction in recurring meetings | 47% (28 to 66) |
| Improvement in fatigue | 18% (2 to 34) |
| Unexplained | 35% |

The meetings pathway, first suggested in the nine-month report's exploratory analysis and since dismissed as post hoc, survives a registered test with a larger sample of office-months and a pre-specified model. Reduced fatigue contributes, but less than half as much. About a third of the gain is not explained by either measured pathway.

### An unplanned observation

In month 15, two control offices, on their own initiative and without changing hours, carried out a "meeting audit" and cancelled a number of standing meetings. Recurring meeting time in those two offices fell from 7.1 to 5.0 hours per week, and their output per hour over the following six months was 4.1% above their own previous six months. This is two offices, uncontrolled, and the change was smaller than in treated offices. It suggests, without establishing, that part of the per-hour gain might be available without reducing hours. Whether reorganisation alone could capture most of the gain, or whether the hours cut is what makes such reorganisation happen and stick, cannot be determined from this trial, since no arm reorganised without reducing hours.

## 4. Halden organisations at 24 months

We contacted the 23 Halden organisations that had submitted output records; 14 agreed to provide 24-month data. Three of these had reverted to a five-day schedule: a hospitality group and a retail chain, both citing coverage of opening hours, and a marketing agency citing client deadlines. Their record-based output indices at the time of reversion were between 88 and 91.

Among the 11 that continued, record-based output at 24 months stood at 96.8 against the pre-pilot baseline, and actual hours from time tracking at 34.9 against 40.3 (−13.4%), an implied gain in output per actual hour of 11.8%. These organisations have no comparison group and are survivors twice over: they completed the pilot and then chose to continue. Their figures are an upper bound for organisations that self-select into reduced hours and find it suits them, not an estimate for organisations in general.

## 5. Bearing on earlier claims

**The re-analysis's claim that per-hour gains are entirely an artifact.** The Varden 24-month estimate uses record-based output, log-measured hours, randomised comparison and a two-year horizon, the standards that re-analysis itself recommended, and finds a gain of 8.5% (3.4 to 13.8). The re-analysis was right about the measurement problems it identified and right that headline figures were inflated; its conclusion that nothing remains once those problems are corrected is not supported.

**The meta-analysis's claim that effects show no sign of decay.** The four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months, listed in the meta-analysis's supplementary table, were all uncontrolled and all used scheduled hours. Their pooled estimate therefore reflects the design features the meta-analysis itself found to inflate effects, and it cannot speak to decay. In the one controlled study with long follow-up, this one, the per-hour gain declined by about a quarter between nine and 24 months.

## 6. Limitations

One public employer; seven offices per arm in the case-processing stratum. Mediation analysis assumes no unmeasured confounding between mediators and outcome, which a cluster trial cannot guarantee. The Halden subset is small and self-selected. Neither source extends beyond 24 months.

response:
# Review of the 24-Month Follow-up of the Varden Trial and Halden Subset

This is the strongest document in the series, and it closes several open questions properly:
- **Pre-registration.** The mediation test was registered at month 11, before the 24-month outcomes existed.
- **Baseline meeting data.** Calendar data now include a baseline: treated offices 7.4, control 7.2 hours a week. That rules out the possibility that the month-6 meeting gap reflected pre-existing differences between offices.
- **Appeal censoring.** At 24 months, appeals against decisions made around month 9 have had time to resolve. The overturn comparison is no longer limited by appeals still pending.
- **Ending the counter arm.** Stopping it at month 12, with a stated cost rationale, settles what happens in coverage-bound work.
- **Section 5.** The rebuttal to the meta-analysis is correct and important. If its four long-follow-up studies were all uncontrolled and used scheduled hours, they can't speak to decay.

The arithmetic is consistent:
- 0.966/0.88 = +9.8% (timesheets) and 0.966/0.89 = +8.5% (logs).
- Halden's continuing organisations: 96.8/86.6 = +11.8%.
- The mediation shares sum to 100%.
- The confidence intervals are symmetric on the log scale.

The problems are mainly about interpretation: what the log measure captures, how strong the mediation claim is, contamination of the control group, and a few inconsistencies.

## 1. The Summary's decline figure mixes two hours measures

The Summary says the gain "fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months." The 12.5% is on timesheets and the 8.5% is on system logs. The like-for-like change on timesheets is 12.5% to 9.8%, a decline of about 22%. Mixing measures makes it look like 32%. Section 5's "about a quarter" is closer to right. Use the timesheet comparison in the Summary and report the log figure separately.

The two confidence intervals also overlap substantially (+6.9 to +18.4 versus +4.6 to +15.2). "Consistent with some fading" is fair, but report a formal test of the change, with the uncertainty in each estimate taken into account. The decline itself isn't statistically established.

## 2. What the system-log measure captures

Active log-in time on the case-management system records casework. It almost certainly does not record meetings, email, phone calls or other work done outside the system. So it is not a "stricter" measure of total working time. It measures a different denominator, casework time. This matters in three ways:

- **What output per log-hour means.** It measures productivity while working on cases. That makes it a strong measure of efficiency at casework, but it doesn't reflect time freed from meetings and reallocated to cases.
- **What the mediation result means.** If meetings fall outside log time, cutting meetings doesn't mechanically raise output per log-hour. A 47% mediation share would then imply something other than "more time available for cases." Possibilities include fewer interruptions, less fragmented work, or general reorganisation. Spell out which interpretation you intend.
- **Pre-period data.** Table 1 reports a difference-in-differences estimate for log hours, which requires pre-period log data. The text says the measure was "added" at follow-up. Confirm that baseline log data were extracted retrospectively for both arms.

Please define precisely what counts as active log-in time, including how idle time is handled, and state whether meeting time is excluded.

## 3. The mediation result: "confirms" is too strong

- **Mediation is observational even within a randomised trial.** Randomisation identifies the effect of the schedule. It does not identify the effect of meetings on output. The limitation is acknowledged, but the Summary says "confirms," and that word should go.
- **The meetings mediator may be a proxy.** Managers who cut meetings hardest probably also simplified approvals, protected focus time and dropped low-value reporting, as the Halden interviews describe. Without measuring those, "meetings" may stand in for reorganisation generally. The 47% is better described as "meetings and correlated reorganisation."
- **The precision looks too good for 14 offices.** Treatment varies only between 14 offices, and office-months within an office are not independent. A proportion-mediated estimate whose denominator (a total effect of 8.5%, CI 3.4 to 13.8) is itself uncertain usually has a very wide interval. An interval of 28–66% seems narrow for this design. Report how the intervals were obtained: cluster bootstrap, how many clusters were resampled, and whether 14 clusters were adequate. Also give an interval for the unexplained 35%.
- **This is a replication in the same offices.** The hypothesis came from the same seven treated offices. Months 10–24 are new data, but this is weaker than replication in a new sample. Say so, especially when responding to Varga & Holm's "does not replicate" critique.

## 4. The control-office meeting audit contaminates the comparison

Two of the seven control offices cut meetings in month 15. This has two consequences the report doesn't draw out:

- **Part of the apparent "fading" may be control improvement.** If those offices' output per hour rose about 4%, the control average rose by roughly 1.2 points (2 of 7 offices). The treated–control gap would shrink by about that much without any decline in treated offices. Part of the drop from 12.5% to 9.8% may therefore come from the control group improving. Report the 24-month estimates excluding those two offices, or using only months before 15, as a sensitivity analysis.
- **The control meeting figures don't add up.** If two offices fell from 7.1 to 5.0 hours (−2.1 each), the seven-office control average should fall by about 0.6 hours. The report says it moved from 7.2 to 7.0. Either the other five control offices increased meeting time by about 0.4 hours on average, or the figures need checking.

The audit may also be a spillover from the trial itself, for example if control managers read the nine-month report. If so, the comparison is contaminated rather than showing an independent phenomenon. The caution in "suggests, without establishing" is appropriate for the uncontrolled before–after comparison, which is also open to regression to the mean and seasonality.

## 5. Halden subset

- **The marketing agency doesn't fit the Summary's framing.** The Summary says all three reversions were organisations "with client-facing or coverage obligations." But the marketing agency cited *client deadlines*, which is discretionary work. Folding it into "client-facing" blurs the distinction the whole literature now relies on. This is a discretionary-work failure and should be reported as one.
- **Check the baseline hours figure.** The 11 continuing organisations' baseline of 40.3 hours is identical to the 27-organisation average in Varga & Holm. The 17-organisation subset there was 40.4. Confirm this is the 11 organisations' own baseline and not a reused figure.
- **Selection.** Nine of the 23 organisations contacted declined to provide data, on top of earlier attrition.
- **"Upper bound" is not quite right.** With no comparison group, background trends could push the figure either way. "Optimistic estimate for organisations that self-select and persist" is more accurate.
- **Include the reverters.** Reporting a summary across all 14 organisations, counting the 3 reverters at their output at reversion (88–91), would give a less selected picture.

## 6. Counter-arm cost figure

Restoring output would need about 1/0.886 ≈ 13% more staff, which matches the stated 12%. But with pay unchanged per person, 12% more staff for the same contacts means labour cost per contact rises by about 12%, not 9%. The 9% presumably reflects non-labour costs in the denominator. State that assumption.

## 7. Smaller points

- **Few clusters.** Inference still rests on 7 versus 7 offices. Report wild-cluster-bootstrap or randomisation-inference results for the main 24-month estimates.
- **Sick days and resignations.** These still lack confidence intervals. Sick days are not adjusted per scheduled day.
- **The rebuttal to the novelty extrapolation is too direct.** That extrapolation concerned self-reported energy in self-selected Halden organisations. Varden's persistence in a public employer that didn't volunteer weakens the novelty argument but doesn't directly refute a claim about a different population. Varga & Holm's line also reached zero nearer month 9 than month 10.
- **Authorship.** Two of the questions examined are the authors' own: the Varden team's meetings hypothesis, and the Halden pilot via Okafor. A brief statement on this would help readers, given that the paper adjudicates critiques of both.
- **Policy-relevant result.** Output per employee at 24 months (−3.4%, CI −8.0 to +1.2) is drifting slightly downward. It deserves more emphasis than "mostly offset," because it is the figure that determines whether the change pays for itself in discretionary work.

## Summary

| Claim | Assessment |
|---|---|
| Per-hour gain persists at 24 months (~8.5–9.8%) | Well supported; inference with 14 clusters still needs a robustness check |
| Gain fell from 12.5% to 8.5% | Mixes measures; the timesheet figure (9.8%) is like-for-like, and contamination may explain part of the fall |
| Log hours are the stricter measure | Unclear; logs likely measure casework time only |
| Meetings mediate 47% ("confirms") | Supportive, not confirmatory; mediator may proxy broader reorganisation; intervals look narrow |
| Fatigue contributes 18% | Plausible, with the same caveats |
| Not "entirely an artifact" | Well supported by the randomised 24-month estimate |
| Meta-analysis's "no decay" claim unsupported | Correct |
| Halden reversions all coverage/client-facing | Overstated; the marketing agency is a discretionary-work reversion |
| Halden continuers +11.8% | Optimistic, selected estimate; check the baseline figure |

## Suggested revisions

1. Report the timesheet-to-timesheet decline in the Summary, together with a test of the change.
2. Define log-in time precisely, and confirm pre-period log data exist for both arms.
3. Replace "confirms" with "supports," explain how the mediation intervals were computed, and discuss correlated reorganisation as an alternative explanation.
4. Add a sensitivity analysis excluding the two audited control offices, and reconcile the control meeting averages.
5. Reclassify the marketing-agency reversion and add an all-14 summary for the Halden subset.
6. Add small-cluster inference and a short author-involvement statement.

The core conclusion holds up: in discretionary work, a real per-hour gain of roughly 8–10% persists at two years under rigorous measurement, and coverage-bound work does not pay for itself. The changes above would make the mechanism and decay claims as solid as the main result.
